# CIVA downgrades

These descriptions are generated from the Tuning package of FCScore and describe what FCScore measures for each downgrade. See the [downgrade reference](index.md) for how to read them.

Generated from Tuning commit: `5e395b4`.

**Rulebook source**

> - [FAI Sporting Code Section 6 Part 1, Powered Aircraft, Version 2026-2](https://www.civanews.com/wp-content/uploads/Section6_Part1_2026_v2.pdf)
>
> This configuration is for powered aircraft in the Unlimited, Advanced and Intermediate categories, flown in the 1000 m performance zone.
>
> The judging references in `judging_guide.json` are verbatim extracts from CIVA-P, identified by their paragraph number: the performance zone and height rules in Chapter 3 (3.3.1.1, 3.8.1.1), the downgrades and penalties in Chapter 4 (4.3.5, 4.3.6, 4.4.1) and the criteria for judging aerobatic figures in Appendix B (B.3 to B.9). The zone and height limits are contest penalties in the rules rather than figure deductions, so the FCScore box downgrades are estimates of their severity.
>
> CIVA-P and the IAC rules are related but not identical. Where CIVA-P gives a four point deduction (a spin that never stalls, a snap without clearly seen autorotation, a tailslide with no backwards slide) the corresponding FCScore downgrades are weighted at about four points, and FCScore does not model the CIVA-P rule that a snap whose autorotation ends with more than 45° of rotation remaining scores zero.
>
> The Positioning references (4.1.5.1 to 4.1.5.8, B.10) are the sequence-level positioning mark, which has its own K factor. FCScore models it from the box deductions of all the figures, not from the judges' 'Pos' annotations.

Rulebook extracts are quoted verbatim and listed under [Rulebook references](#rulebook-references).

## Intra-element downgrades

### Horizontal Line Climb {#climb}

`climb`

Checks that horizontal lines are flown at constant altitude, with no climb or descent in the flight path. Only growth in the climb or descent angle is charged, so returning to level flight is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Horizontal lines must be flown at a constant altitude and are judged on the flight path rather than the attitude, because the attitude needed for level flight varies with aircraft type and airspeed. The line should look level whatever angle the nose is held at.

    FCScore measures the angle between the aircraft's flight path and the horizontal over each horizontal line and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. A climb or descent already present when the line starts was charged on the element that created it, so it is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Horizontal lines in the vertical plane are judged on flight path, not attitude. … The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> All deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank), and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.4.1.4](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Horizontal Line Heading {#heading}

`heading`

Checks that the nose stays parallel to the box axis on horizontal lines. Only growth in the heading error is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    On horizontal lines the aircraft's heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis of the box. A pilot may correct for wind drift, but if the correction is visible to the judge the standard deduction of one point per 5° of heading deviation applies.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage, not the flight path, relative to the template heading in the horizontal plane, and charges each increase in the absolute angle over the line; a decrease is free. Because the nose direction is measured, a visible crab against a crosswind shows up here, but only the part that builds up during the line is charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the main or secondary axis.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.heading)

> A common flight mode is to crab into the wind as is done in navigational flight. … The downside to this approach is that if the aircraft longitudinal axis is detected by the Judge to be at an angle to the competition axis (main or secondary), a deduction of one (1) point per five (5) degrees will be given.
>
> [B.7.1.5](#rb-general.wind_correction)

### Vertical/45° Line Yaw {#yaw}

`yaw`

Checks that the nose does not swing sideways on vertical and 45° lines. Only growth in the sideways attitude error is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Vertical and 45° lines are judged on the attitude of the aircraft, according to its zero-lift axis, not on the flight path, so wind drift is ignored but the aircraft must point exactly along the line. The wings must also stay aligned with a box axis and the horizon.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage relative to the template line in the sideways (yaw) direction and charges each increase in the absolute angle over the line; a decrease is free. It uses the fuselage centre-line as the reference rather than your zero-lift axis, which it does not know. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. … The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> This is the vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees. … The prescribed deduction is one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation from the correct geometry (0.5 points per 2.5 degrees).
>
> [B.3.3.1](#rb-lines.diagonal)

### Turn Altitude Change {#axial_track}

`axial_track`

Checks that turns hold a constant altitude. Only growth in the climb or descent angle of the flight path around the turn is charged, so returning to level flight is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In turns and rolling turns the altitude must be constant: a change costs one point for every 5° or 100 feet. Wind effects on a turn are not downgraded, but the pilot must still hold the turn level.

    FCScore measures the angle between the flight path and the horizontal plane of the turn, and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. It applies to horizontal arcs such as turns and rolling turns, and not to loops in a vertical plane. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The aircraft must maintain a constant altitude throughout the figure. Any variation would be either one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of change or one (1) point for every 100 feet.
>
> [B.9.2.5 d](#rb-turns.altitude)

### Loop Plane Attitude {#axial_attitude}

`axial_attitude`

Checks that the nose stays in the plane of the loop. Only growth in the out-of-plane angle of the fuselage is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A looping line is a vertically curving path that must have a constant radius. Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing, and the wings must be level at all times, at one point for every 5° of error in either case.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage out of the plane of the loop and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. It measures the direction the nose points, so a crab angle held against a crosswind shows up here, even though the rules give no deduction for the loop's finish being displaced sideways by crosswind. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing and wings must be level at all times. The one (1) point for every five (5) degrees rule holds for both these cases.
>
> [B.9.10.2](#rb-loops.crab_wings)

### Loop Exit Flight Path {#radial_track}

`radial_track`

Checks that the flight path is exactly level when a loop returns to horizontal flight. The full angle error at the end of the loop is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    When a looping line returns to a horizontal line, that line is judged on flight path, so the loop must finish with the flight path exactly horizontal, with no extra or missing degrees of arc.

    FCScore takes the last point of the loop and charges the whole angle between the flight path and the template within the plane of the loop. It is an absolute measure at the end of the loop, so an over- or under-flown arc is charged here once and the line that follows is only charged for further change. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Horizontal lines in the vertical plane are judged on flight path, not attitude. … The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> All deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank), and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>

??? note "Details"

### Roll Angle on Lines {#line_roll}

`line_roll`

Checks that the wings stay aligned on lines without a roll, and that there is no rolling during a stall turn or tailslide. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so levelling the wings again is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    On vertical lines the wings must remain parallel to the horizon, at one point for every 5° of deviation, and during a stall turn the wings must stay in the vertical plane with no pitch or roll (torquing), at one point for every 5°. The tailslide criteria are those of the hammerhead, so a tailslide is judged in the same way.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on lines that contain no roll, and through stall turns and tailslides, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the element is not charged again, as it was charged where it arose. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> During the vertical climb or vertical descent, the wings must remain parallel to the horizon. There will be a one (1) point deduction per five (5) degrees of deviation of the vertical (yaw) axis from horizontal.
>
> [B.9.5.2 d](#rb-lines.vertical_wings)

> The wings must remain in the vertical geometric plane throughout the turnaround, and the aircraft's attitude before and after the turnaround must be absolutely vertical, with no pitch or roll. If there is movement around the roll axis, often referred to as "torquing" (Figure 22), there is a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees off axis.
>
> [B.9.5.2 g](#rb-stall_turns.pivot_motion)

`loop_roll`

??? note "Details"

    A loop without a roll should be flown with the wings in the plane of the loop, with no bank. Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing and the wings level at all times, at one point for every 5° of error.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template in vertical loops that contain no roll, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the loop is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing and wings must be level at all times. The one (1) point for every five (5) degrees rule holds for both these cases.
>
> [B.9.10.2](#rb-loops.crab_wings)

### Roll Angle in Rolling Turn Pauses {#circle_pause_roll}

`circle_pause_roll`

Checks that the wings stay at the template attitude during a brief pause between the rolls of a rolling turn. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so returning to the attitude is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A rolling turn may pause briefly where the roll direction changes. At a reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level; a longer pause costs up to one point and errors in the roll angle from wings level cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on the short level loop segments that sit between two rolling segments of a turn, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the pause is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At a roll direction reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level. A longer pause is no more than a one (1) point deduction. Errors in the roll angle from wings level are deducted using one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.3.6 e](#rb-turns.rolling_reversal)

### Bank Angle in Turns {#turn_roll}

`turn_roll`

Checks that the bank angle established for a turn is held. Only growth in the bank angle error during the turn is charged, so returning to the bank is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Once the bank angle of a turn has been established it must not change: any change costs one point for every 5°. The bank must be at least 60° when the heading change begins.

    FCScore measures how the bank angle differs from the angle established at the start of the turn, taking an established bank below 60° or above 90° as 60° or 90°, and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. It applies to turns that contain no roll. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The angle of bank, once established, must remain constant. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [B.9.2.5 b](#rb-turns.bank)

> This must be a roll of between 60 and 90 degrees, it must be performed on the entry heading, and the aircraft must maintain a constant horizontal line. … The angle of bank established by the initial rolling manoeuvre must be at least 60 degrees. Anything less is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a](#rb-turns.entry_bank)

### Roll Rotation Amount {#roll_roll}

`roll_roll`

Checks that a roll, snap or spin finishes at the planned attitude. At the point of maximum rotation, the roll attitude is compared with the planned attitude and the difference is charged once, so both over- and under-rotation count. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A roll must end with a precise stop, with the wings at the desired degree of rotation, and an error in the extent of rotation, including over-rotation, costs one point for every 5°. A snap (flick roll) must likewise stop at the desired extent of roll, and a spin on its pre-stated heading.

    FCScore finds the point of maximum rotation in each roll, snap or spin and compares the aircraft's roll attitude there with the planned attitude. It assesses the final attitude, not the total number of degrees rolled, although it tracks the rotation continuously (allowing for the angle wrapping round at 180°) so that a roll that overshoots by a full turn is not mistaken for a correct one. Over-rotation and under-rotation are charged equally, as a single absolute error at that point. Rolling back afterwards is charged separately, and the over-rotation is not charged a second time when the pilot corrects it. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The wings must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as "bumping the point". A deduction of half (0.5) point to one (1) point is given depending on the severity of the "bump".
>
> [B.9.25.3](#rb-rolls.stop)

> Over-rotating a roll and rolling the wings back again must be penalised by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of over-rotation, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards, and no matter how quickly the correction is made.
>
> [4.4.1.5](#rb-general.corrections)

### Turn Entry Bank Angle {#preturn_roll}

`preturn_roll`

Checks that the roll into a turn establishes at least 60° of bank. Any shortfall below 60° at the end of the roll is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A competition turn starts with a roll on the entry heading that establishes the bank, before the heading change begins. CIVA-P describes this as a roll of between 60° and 90°, but only a bank of less than 60° is deducted, at one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the point of maximum rotation of the roll that precedes a turn, measures the bank angle from wings level, and charges any amount by which it is below 60°. A bank of more than 60° is not charged here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> This must be a roll of between 60 and 90 degrees, it must be performed on the entry heading, and the aircraft must maintain a constant horizontal line. … The angle of bank established by the initial rolling manoeuvre must be at least 60 degrees. Anything less is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a](#rb-turns.entry_bank)

### Roll Rebound {#rebound}

`rebound`

Checks that a roll stays where it stopped. After the maximum rotation, any growth in the roll error, such as bouncing back past the target or wobbling, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The wings must stop precisely after the desired rotation and not go past the stop point and then return, which is called bumping the point. An over-rotation is penalised by one point for every 5°, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards and however quickly the correction is made; FCScore charges it once and does not charge it again for rolling back.

    FCScore looks at each rotating element after the point of maximum rotation and charges each increase in the absolute roll error. An over-rotation is charged once, at the point of maximum rotation, so rolling back from it is not charged again, but rolling back past the target or rocking the wings creates a new increase that is charged. A decrease in the error is free. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Over-rotating a roll and rolling the wings back again must be penalised by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of over-rotation, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards, and no matter how quickly the correction is made.
>
> [4.4.1.5](#rb-general.corrections)

> The wings must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as "bumping the point". A deduction of half (0.5) point to one (1) point is given depending on the severity of the "bump".
>
> [B.9.25.3](#rb-rolls.stop)

### Roll Centring on the Loop {#loop_roll_centre}

`loop_roll_centre`

Checks that a roll, or roll combination, on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A roll or rolls at the apex of a loop must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. The pilot chooses how much of the loop the roll or roll combination uses, but it must take the same amount of loop before the apex as after it. A roll that is off centre costs one point for every 5° of arc it is off centre.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centred.
>
> [B.9.10.3](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Snap Centring on the Loop {#loop_snap_centre}

`loop_snap_centre`

Checks that a snap roll on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A snap roll on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The snap is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the snap into it. A loop whose only roll is a snap is scored in the same way, with the snap centred on the apex.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centred.
>
> [B.9.10.3](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Pause Centring on the Loop {#loop_pause_centre}

`loop_pause_centre`

Checks that a pause between rolls on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A pause between two rolls or snaps on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The pause is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the pause into it. The pads of the loop before and after the rolling section are not part of it.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centred.
>
> [B.9.10.3](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Roll Rate Consistency {#roll_rate}

`roll_rate`

Checks that the roll rate is constant through each roll. The size of the variation in roll rate, compared with the average, is charged once for the roll. Small variations are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, and for short part-rolls that give less to judge.

??? note "Details"

    Rolls must be flown at a constant roll rate: any variance costs one point, for example slowing sharply for the last 45° of a 180° roll. Rolling turns are judged in the same way.

    FCScore measures the roll rate throughout each roll and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. A steady roll scores zero, whatever its rate. The more the rate varies, the larger the downgrade. FCScore charges in proportion to the variation, not in whole points per occurrence.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting also grows with the amount of roll flown: a full roll or more counts fully, a half roll counts about half, because short rolls give the judge less to assess. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors.

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the slow roll that could result in its being considered a hesitation roll, would Hard Zero (HZ) the figure.
>
> [B.9.25.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> Each variation in the rate of roll is no more than a one (1) point deduction.
>
> [B.9.3.6 d](#rb-turns.rolling_rate)

### Roll Pauses {#roll_excitation}

`roll_excitation`

Checks that the roll does not stop partway. The share of the roll for which the roll rate is close to zero, or reversed, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    The rate of roll must not stop in a slow roll or a rolling turn, apart from a short pause when changing roll direction. A stoppage in a slow roll that could be taken for a hesitation roll is a hard zero, and each stoppage of the roll in a rolling turn costs two points. FCScore grades the share of the roll spent stopped rather than awarding a hard zero.

    FCScore counts the time during each roll in which the roll rate is effectively zero or reversed. A rate below about 1.5° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 3° per second counts as moving, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the roll's duration spent stopped, so a long hold costs more than a brief one.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the slow roll that could result in its being considered a hesitation roll, would Hard Zero (HZ) the figure.
>
> [B.9.25.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of two (2) points. … At a roll direction reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level. A longer pause is no more than a one (1) point deduction.
>
> [B.9.3.6 d, B.9.3.6 e](#rb-turns.rolling_stop)

### Loop Roundness {#radius}

`radius`

Checks that each loop is round, with a constant radius throughout. The variation of the radius within the loop, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, high or wide in the box, and part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius. The judge divides the loop into quadrants and downgrades any recognizable variation in the radius by up to two points per quadrant, depending on the magnitude of the variation.

    FCScore fits a circle to the flown path of the loop in the plane of the loop and measures how much the aircraft's distance from the fitted centre varies, as a fraction of the average radius. A perfectly round loop scores zero, whatever its size, and the more the radius varies the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Shape errors are easiest to see when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where distortions are hidden. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter. Large errors are counted in full.

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.
>
> [B.8.2.1 a](#rb-loops.radius)

> To better quantify deductions for irregularity of the radius of looping figures, the Judge divides the loop into quadrants. Any recognizable variation in the radius must be downgraded by a maximum of two (2) points per quadrant depending on the magnitude of the variation.
>
> [B.9.10.4](#rb-loops.radius_deductions)

### Flat Spots in Loops {#radius_excitation}

`radius_excitation`

Checks that the loop has no straight sections. The share of the loop for which the flight path is effectively straight is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius, and where a roll is integrated into a loop any part of the roll flown on a straight line costs at least two points.

    FCScore watches the curvature of the flight path through the loop and counts the time during which it is effectively straight, or curving the wrong way. A local radius of about 1000 m or more counts as fully flat and about 500 m or less counts as curved, with values in between counting partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the loop's duration that is flat.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.
>
> [B.8.2.1 a](#rb-loops.radius)

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centred.
>
> [B.9.10.3](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Loop Rate of Turn {#curvature}

`curvature`

Checks that the loop keeps a steady rate of turn for its speed. The variation in the loop's curvature, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius, which means the aircraft has to turn at a steady rate for its speed, neither tightening nor opening up as it goes round.

    FCScore measures the rate of turn divided by the speed of travel (the curvature, which is one over the radius) throughout the loop and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. Because it is based on how quickly the aircraft is turning for its speed, it picks up a tightening or opening of the loop early. The more the curvature varies, the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.
>
> [B.8.2.1 a](#rb-loops.radius)

### Spin Rotation Axis {#spin_rotation_axis}

`spin_rotation_axis`

Checks that the spin is a true autorotation. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 25°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A spin is graded on a clean breaking stall in horizontal flight and a fully stalled autorotation. If the aircraft never stalls, or a barrel roll or flick roll is offered as a simulated spin, the figure is downgraded by four points. During autorotation pitch angle and rotation rate may vary without penalty, so only the type of rotation matters.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the break to 45° before the end of the rotation. Any period in which it is below 25° looks like a roll about the fuselage rather than an autorotation and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the spin it covers. The 25° threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules. Where CIVA-P gives a four point deduction for a spin that is not a stalled autorotation, FCScore grades the check: it is weighted at four points for each 15° by which the rotation axis is below the threshold, and scaled by the share of the spin affected.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> In all spins the grading criteria are: a) A clean breaking stall in horizontal flight. b) Fully stalled autorotation. c) Stopping on pre-stated heading. d) Vertical down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading. e) A constant, reasonable quarter-loop radius back the horizontal flight.
>
> [B.9.29.7](#rb-spins.definition)

> Throughout the flick the roll must be driven primarily by the rudder, and autorotation must be seen to continue. This can best be confirmed by the observed conical motion of the fuselage longitudinal axis, the largest displacement being at the tail which is furthest from the C of G.
>
> [B.9.27.4](#rb-general.autorotation)

### Spin Nose Drop {#drop_pitch_rate}

`drop_pitch_rate`

Checks that the nose drops as the aircraft stalls into the spin. Time spent dropping slower than 6° per second in the first 15° of rotation is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: with the aircraft high or wide in the box, or directly above the judge.

??? note "Details"

    When the aircraft stalls, the nose will fall and at the same time the wing tip will drop in the direction of the spin. Failure to achieve this is a forced entry and costs one point for every 5° of deviation. If the aircraft never stalls it cannot spin, and the figure is downgraded by four points.

    FCScore measures the nose-down pitch rate from the start of the spin until the first 15° of rotation is complete. Any period below 6° per second is charged, according to how far below it is and how large a share of that window it covers. The 6° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a definite nose drop, not a number from the rules. A spin with no nose drop at all costs about four points here.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The nose drop is harder to see when the aircraft is directly above the judge, and when it is high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error. Large errors are counted in full.

> When the aircraft stalls, the nose will fall and at the same time the wing tip will drop in the direction of the spin. Failure to achieve this should be considered a "forced entry" and downgraded one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation. … If the aircraft never stalls, it is apparent that it cannot spin, and a downgrade of four (4) points must be given.
>
> [B.9.29.3, B.9.29.6](#rb-spins.entry)

### Spin Rotation Hesitation {#spin_excitation}

`spin_excitation`

Checks that the spin keeps rotating. The share of the spin for which the rotation rate is very low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must continue throughout the spin. If the autorotation stops early and the aircraft is then aileroned round to the pre-stated heading, one point is deducted for every 5° of ailerons used.

    FCScore counts the time in each spin during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is close to zero or reversed. A rate below about 9° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 17° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the spin's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Be alert for early stopping of the stalled autorotation followed by "aileroning" to the pre-stated heading. In this case, a deduction of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of "aileroning" must be applied.
>
> [B.9.29.4](#rb-spins.continue)

### Spin Exit Pitch Attitude {#spin_exit_pitch}

`spin_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft ends the spin pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch angle error of the fuselage at the end of the spin is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed number of turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, and a vertical (90° down), wings-level attitude must then be seen. Errors cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole angle between the fuselage and the template downline in the pitch direction. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Vertical down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.
>
> [B.9.29.7 d](#rb-spins.downline)

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, then a 90 degree down, wings-level attitude must be seen.
>
> [B.9.29.4](#rb-spins.stop)

### Spin Exit Sideways Lean {#spin_exit_yaw}

`spin_exit_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft ends the spin pointing vertically down, not leaning to the side. The full sideways angle error of the fuselage at the end of the spin is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed number of turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, and a vertical (90° down), wings-level attitude must then be seen. Alignment errors cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole sideways angle between the fuselage and the template downline. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, then a 90 degree down, wings-level attitude must be seen.
>
> [B.9.29.4](#rb-spins.stop)

> Vertical down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.
>
> [B.9.29.7 d](#rb-spins.downline)

### Snap Rotation Axis {#snap_rotation_axis}

`snap_rotation_axis`

Checks that the snap is a true autorotation rather than an axial roll. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 10°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A flick (snap) roll is a rudder-driven autorotation, confirmed by the conical motion of the fuselage axis, so the rotation should not be a simple roll about the fuselage line. If the pitch change or the autorotation is not clearly seen, the mark is downgraded by four points.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the start of the rotation to 90° before its end. Any period in which it is below 10° looks like an aileron roll and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the snap it covers. The threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules. Where CIVA-P gives a four point deduction for a flick that is not clearly an autorotation, FCScore grades the check: it is weighted at four points for a rotation that stays at the fuselage axis throughout.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> Either shortly after or simultaneously with the pitch change the aircraft must yaw, initiating a stall of one wing and the rapid onset of autorotation.
>
> [B.9.27.3](#rb-snap_rolls.definition)

> Throughout the flick the roll must be driven primarily by the rudder, and autorotation must be seen to continue. This can best be confirmed by the observed conical motion of the fuselage longitudinal axis, the largest displacement being at the tail which is furthest from the C of G.
>
> [B.9.27.4](#rb-general.autorotation)

### Snap Rotation Hesitation {#snap_excitation}

`snap_excitation`

Checks that the snap keeps rotating. The share of the snap for which the rotation rate is low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must continue throughout the flick. If it ceases before the end of the roll, one point is deducted for each 5° of rotation remaining. If it ends with more than 45° remaining, even if the roll is completed with aileron, the flick roll is awarded a numerical zero (0.0).

    FCScore counts the time in each snap during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is low. A rate below about 30° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 57° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the snap's duration spent stopped. FCScore does not model the 45° cut-off: a snap that stops early is charged in proportion to the share of the snap spent stopped and never receives the numerical zero.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> A common error is for the aircraft initially to autorotate but to not stay in autorotation until the end of the figure, the roll becoming driven substantially by application of aileron; in this case a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees of rotation remaining when the autorotation ceases must be made. If autorotation ends with more than 45 degrees of rotation remaining, even if the roll is completed with aileron, the flick roll is awarded a numerical zero (0.0).
>
> [B.9.27.5](#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation)

### Positive Snap Pitch Break {#pos_break_pr}

`pos_break_pr`

Checks that a positive snap starts with a clear pitch break. If the peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation never reaches 30° per second, the shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    To show a positive flick roll has been correctly initiated the judge must see a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude in the nose up / tail down sense, followed by yaw and the rapid onset of autorotation. If the required pitch change or the autorotation is not clearly seen, the mark is downgraded by four points; pitching the wrong way is a hard zero.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and takes its largest absolute value. If that peak never reaches 30° per second the shortfall is charged. The 30° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a clear break, not a number from the rules, and only the peak counts. A snap with no pitch break at all costs about four points here, graded by the shortfall.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> The judge must see two things to determine that a flick roll has been correctly initiated: a) the aircraft must display a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude (Figure 48) to put the wing close to the stall, and b) autorotation must be initiated by use of the rudder. … However, if the required pitch change and/or actual autorotation are not clearly seen, the mark must be downgraded by four (4) points. … At the start of a positive flick roll, the aircraft must clearly and unambiguously pitch in the nose up / tail down sense, from the pilot’s perspective, to put the wings near the critical angle-of-attack (Figure 48). If the aircraft pitches in the wrong direction, a Hard Zero (HZ) is given.
>
> [B.9.27.2, B.9.27.3](#rb-snap_rolls.break)

### Negative Snap Pitch Break {#neg_break_pr}

`neg_break_pr`

Checks that a negative snap starts with a clear pitch break. The peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation is compared with a 30° per second threshold and any shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A negative flick roll uses the same criteria as a positive one except that the nose and tail must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense. If the nose moves the wrong way it is not a negative flick and the figure is a hard zero; a pitch change that is not clearly seen is downgraded by four points.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and compares its absolute value with a 30° per second threshold, charging any shortfall. The threshold is an FCScore value for a clear break, not a number from the rules. A snap with no pitch break at all costs about four points here, graded by the shortfall.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> For negative flick rolls, all criteria stated for positive flick rolls apply except that the aircraft is in a negative rather than positive angle-of-attack during autorotation. Therefore, in a negative flick roll the nose and tail of the aircraft must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense, from the pilot’s perspective, as the angle-of-attack is changed (Figure 49).
>
> [B.9.28.1](#rb-snap_rolls.negative)

> The judge must see two things to determine that a flick roll has been correctly initiated: a) the aircraft must display a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude (Figure 48) to put the wing close to the stall, and b) autorotation must be initiated by use of the rudder. … However, if the required pitch change and/or actual autorotation are not clearly seen, the mark must be downgraded by four (4) points. … At the start of a positive flick roll, the aircraft must clearly and unambiguously pitch in the nose up / tail down sense, from the pilot’s perspective, to put the wings near the critical angle-of-attack (Figure 48). If the aircraft pitches in the wrong direction, a Hard Zero (HZ) is given.
>
> [B.9.27.2, B.9.27.3](#rb-snap_rolls.break)

### Snap Exit Pitch Attitude {#snap_exit_pitch}

`snap_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft returns to the correct pitch attitude after a snap on a vertical or 45° line. Only growth in the pitch error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°. A lateral or vertical displacement of the path caused by the snap is not charged provided the path stays parallel.

    FCScore compares the fuselage pitch relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the attitude closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. It applies to snaps that do not finish on a horizontal line. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> For all aircraft types, the criteria for stopping the flick roll are the same: autorotation must stop at the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by adoption of the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. … Downgrades for errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of error.
>
> [B.9.27.4](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> For all aircraft types, the criteria for stopping the flick roll are the same: autorotation must stop at the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by adoption of the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. … Downgrades for errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of error.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the flight path that fits the underlying figure, and horizontal lines are judged on flight path. Failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°.

    FCScore compares the flight path angle to the horizontal at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> For all aircraft types, the criteria for stopping the flick roll are the same: autorotation must stop at the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by adoption of the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. … Downgrades for errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of error.

> Horizontal lines in the vertical plane are judged on flight path, not attitude. … The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.

    FCScore compares the fuselage heading relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the heading closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> For all aircraft types, the criteria for stopping the flick roll are the same: autorotation must stop at the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by adoption of the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. … Downgrades for errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of error.

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the main or secondary axis.

### Stall Turn Pivot Width {#width}

`width`

Checks that the aircraft pivots near its centre of gravity at the top of a stall turn. The sideways travel in the direction of the turn beyond an allowance is charged, ignoring downwind drift. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    To avoid a deduction the aircraft must pivot around an axis point no farther from its centre of gravity than half a wingspan, and each additional half wingspan costs one point (flying over the top).

    CIVA-P does not mention wind drift at the pivot; FCScore measures how far the aircraft's centre of gravity moves sideways in the direction of the turn from the start of the stall turn, with movement from drifting downwind removed but upwind drift left in. The largest width beyond a fixed allowance is charged once. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the sideways distance moved in metres with the allowance as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement up to the allowance and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced width that is charged.

> As the aircraft nears the point where it would stop climbing, it must pivot in a plane parallel to vertical. Ideally, the aircraft pivots around its centre of gravity. … The downgrade for this deviation (often referred to as "flying over the top") is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Pivot Point B, Figure 21).
>
> [B.9.5.2 e](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Height Loss {#height}

`height`

Checks that the aircraft does not lose height through the pivot of a stall turn. How far below its highest point the aircraft is at the start and end of the stall turn, beyond an allowance, is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Ideally the aircraft pivots around its centre of gravity. The pivot point may be up to half a wingspan from it without penalty, and each additional half wingspan costs one point. CIVA-P does not treat height lost in the pivot separately, so FCScore applies the same rule to it.

    FCScore measures how far below the highest point of the stall turn the aircraft is at the first and last points of the stall turn element, and charges any height lost beyond a fixed allowance. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

    The results plot shows how far the aircraft is below its highest point, in metres, with the allowance as dashed lines. The judged line follows the measurement inside the allowance and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced height loss that is charged.

> As the aircraft nears the point where it would stop climbing, it must pivot in a plane parallel to vertical. Ideally, the aircraft pivots around its centre of gravity. … The downgrade for this deviation (often referred to as "flying over the top") is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Pivot Point B, Figure 21).
>
> [B.9.5.2 e](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Downline Yaw {#stallturn_exit_yaw}

`stallturn_exit_yaw`

Checks that the downline after a stall turn is not leaning sideways. The full sideways attitude error at the end of the line is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the pivot the aircraft must be established on a vertical downline, which like all vertical lines is judged on attitude, at one point per 5° of error.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line that follows the stall turn and charges the whole sideways angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at the end of the line. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. … The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> As the aircraft nears the point where it would stop climbing, it must pivot in a plane parallel to vertical. Ideally, the aircraft pivots around its centre of gravity. … The downgrade for this deviation (often referred to as "flying over the top") is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Pivot Point B, Figure 21).
>

This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. … The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.
>
> [B.3.2.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> As the aircraft nears the point where it would stop climbing, it must pivot in a plane parallel to vertical. Ideally, the aircraft pivots around its centre of gravity. … The downgrade for this deviation (often referred to as "flying over the top") is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Pivot Point B, Figure 21).
