### Tailslide Sideways Lean {#tailslide_yaw}

`tailslide_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft does not lean sideways during a tailslide. Only growth in the sideways lean of the fuselage is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A tailslide must be flown in the vertical plane and not with the nose inclined towards the horizon, and a slide of that type costs one point for every 5° of inclination. Leaning into the slide on the upline carries into the slide and is deducted there too.

    FCScore measures the lean of the fuselage sideways relative to the template throughout the tailslide and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The aircraft must slide in the vertical plane and not with the nose inclined towards the horizon. A slide of this type must be downgraded by the formula of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of inclination.
>
> [B.9.6.1](#rb-tailslides.lean)

### Tailslide Exit Pitch {#tailslide_exit_pitch}

`tailslide_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft finishes the tailslide pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch attitude error at the end of the tailslide is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the backwards slide the aircraft must tip over and fall through to a diving position. It may swing past the vertical after falling through, which is not downgraded.

    FCScore takes the last point of the tailslide and charges the whole pitch angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at that point, so a swing past the vertical that has settled by then is not charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Following the slide backwards, the aircraft must then tip over and fall through to a diving position.
>
> [B.9.6.2](#rb-tailslides.recovery)

### Tailslide Stop {#tailslide_stop}

`tailslide_stop`

Checks that the aircraft comes to a stop at the top of the vertical line before it slides back. The vertical speed left at the end of the upline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a tailslide the aircraft climbs vertically and stops before sliding backwards, with the backwards slide beginning when upward motion ceases.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line before the tailslide and charges the absolute vertical speed there. A larger speed means the aircraft was still climbing, or already falling, instead of being stopped. The downgrade scale is an FCScore value; the rules do not set a speed limit.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> In summary, the aircraft should make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight, the wings should stay level in relation to the horizon, and the aircraft should come to a complete stop in this attitude.
>
> [B.9.6.6](#rb-tailslides.definition)

### Tailslide Slide Distance {#tailslide_drop}

`tailslide_drop`

Checks that the aircraft slides backwards a visible distance. A slide shorter than 1 m is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    At the point where the aircraft stops, it must slide backwards by at least half a fuselage length. If there is no slide of at least this length, the mark is downgraded by four points.

    FCScore adds up the distance travelled backwards through the tailslide and charges any shortfall below 1 m. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your fuselage length, and charges a graded downgrade that reaches four points when there is no slide at all, matching the CIVA-P four point deduction.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the point when the aircraft stops, it must slide backwards by at least a half fuselage length. If there is no slide of at least this length, the mark is downgraded by four (4) points. … A tail slide that does not move backwards by the required amount must be penalized by four (4) points.
>
> [B.9.6.1, 4.4.1.7](#rb-tailslides.slide)

### Sequence Entry Climb {#seqstart_entry_climb}

`seqstart_entry_climb`

Checks the climb angle before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole angle between the flight path and the horizontal. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the initiation or completion of every figure and at comparable moments within the figure, each deviation from a wings level, horizontal flight path with the aircraft longitudinal axis parallel to the relevant box axis, in accordance with paragraph B.6.1.1, will attract a reduction of half (0.5) point per 2.5 degrees of deviation, one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.4.1.2](#rb-general.figure_start)

> Horizontal lines in the vertical plane are judged on flight path, not attitude. … The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

### Sequence Entry Climb Drift {#seqstart_climb}

`seqstart_climb`

Checks the climb angle stays correct before the first figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore measures the angle between the flight path and the horizontal over the last second of the line before the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the initiation or completion of every figure and at comparable moments within the figure, each deviation from a wings level, horizontal flight path with the aircraft longitudinal axis parallel to the relevant box axis, in accordance with paragraph B.6.1.1, will attract a reduction of half (0.5) point per 2.5 degrees of deviation, one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.4.1.2](#rb-general.figure_start)

> Horizontal lines in the vertical plane are judged on flight path, not attitude. … The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the initiation or completion of every figure and at comparable moments within the figure, each deviation from a wings level, horizontal flight path with the aircraft longitudinal axis parallel to the relevant box axis, in accordance with paragraph B.6.1.1, will attract a reduction of half (0.5) point per 2.5 degrees of deviation, one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.

### Sequence Entry Heading Drift {#seqstart_heading}

`seqstart_heading`

Checks the heading stays correct before the first figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage and the template heading in the horizontal plane, which measures the nose rather than the flight path over the last second of the line before the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at that point, not again here. The window ends where the figure starts and moves with it, so the error cannot be moved out of the score by placing the start of the figure later. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the initiation or completion of every figure and at comparable moments within the figure, each deviation from a wings level, horizontal flight path with the aircraft longitudinal axis parallel to the relevant box axis, in accordance with paragraph B.6.1.1, will attract a reduction of half (0.5) point per 2.5 degrees of deviation, one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.4.1.2](#rb-general.figure_start)

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the main or secondary axis.
>
> [B.8.1.1](#rb-lines.heading)

### Sequence Entry Wings Level {#seqstart_entry_roll}

`seqstart_entry_roll`

Checks the roll angle before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the CIVA-P rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the initiation or completion of every figure and at comparable moments within the figure, each deviation from a wings level, horizontal flight path with the aircraft longitudinal axis parallel to the relevant box axis, in accordance with paragraph B.6.1.1, will attract a reduction of half (0.5) point per 2.5 degrees of deviation, one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.4.1.2](#rb-general.figure_start)

> All deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank), and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [4.4.1.4](#rb-general.angle_rule)

## Positioning (box) downgrades

### Box Ceiling {#top}

`top`

Checks that the figure stays below the top of the aerobatic box. The distance above the ceiling, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    Competitors must obey the height limits for their category: upper limits of 1000 m (Unlimited), 1100 m (Advanced) and 1200 m (Intermediate), and lower limits of 100 m (Unlimited) and 200 m (Advanced and Intermediate). Each climb above the upper limit costs 50 penalty points (Unlimited) or 30 (Advanced and Intermediate). The ceiling depends on the category flown.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is above the ceiling of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch above is charged in proportion to how far above it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

> 4.3.5.1 Unlimited: c) For every climb above the upper height limit (see 3.8.1.1) in Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4, 50 penalty points will be given. … 4.3.5.2 Advanced and Intermediate: c) For every climb above the upper height limit (see 3.8.1.1), 30 penalty points will be given.
>
> [4.3.5.1 c, 4.3.5.2 c](#rb-box.ceiling)

> The following height limitations have been determined for all contest flights: Category Upper Lower Disqualification; Unlimited 1000 m 100 m 50 m; Advanced 1100 m 200 m 100 m; Intermediate 1200 m 200 m 100 m
>
> [3.8.1.1](#rb-box.heights)

### Right Box Boundary {#right}

`right`

Checks that the figure stays inside the the right boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance outside the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    The performance zone is a clearly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m. Each infringement of the zone by more than 50 m costs 30 penalty points (Unlimited) or 20 (Advanced and Intermediate), and every figure started more than 50 m outside the zone is penalised again.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is outside the right boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

> The performance zone (box) must be a clearly and distinctly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m, the central point of which will be the intersection of the axes, as shown in the diagram.
>
> [3.3.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> For each infringement of the performance zone in Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4 by more than 50 metres in the direction of the main axis and/or the secondary axis a pilot will be given penalty points in accordance with the table below. Zone Infringement: Unlimited 30, Advanced or Intermediate 20 (Penalty point tariff). … Thereafter, for every figure started beyond 50 metres outside the performance zone, further penalty points will be given, in accordance with the same table.
>
> [4.3.6.2, 4.3.6.3](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

### Back Box Boundary {#back}

`back`

??? note "Details"

    The performance zone is a clearly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m. Each infringement of the zone by more than 50 m costs 30 penalty points (Unlimited) or 20 (Advanced and Intermediate), and every figure started more than 50 m outside the zone is penalised again. A figure flown where its flight path or attitude cannot reasonably be assessed loses 2 points for each element that cannot be properly assessed.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is beyond the back boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The results plot shows the distance from the judge with the back boundary as a dashed line. The judged line follows the measurement inside the boundary and, beyond it, shows the visibility-reduced distance that is charged.

    The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

> The performance zone (box) must be a clearly and distinctly marked area of 1000 x 1000 m, the central point of which will be the intersection of the axes, as shown in the diagram.
>
> [3.3.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> Should a competitor fly a figure at a location, inside or outside the performance zone, such that the accuracy of the flight path or attitude cannot reasonably be determined, a downgrade of two (2) points should be applied for each element of the figure that cannot be properly assessed.
>
> [B.4.1.3](#rb-box.scorability)

> [3.3.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> For each infringement of the performance zone in Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4 by more than 50 metres in the direction of the main axis and/or the secondary axis a pilot will be given penalty points in accordance with the table below. Zone Infringement: Unlimited 30, Advanced or Intermediate 20 (Penalty point tariff). … Thereafter, for every figure started beyond 50 metres outside the performance zone, further penalty points will be given, in accordance with the same table.
>
> [4.3.6.2, 4.3.6.3](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

### Box Floor {#btm}

`btm`

Checks that the figure stays above the floor of the aerobatic box. The distance below the floor, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged heavily. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted. The deduction is not taken off this figure: it is added to the sequence's Positioning score.

??? note "Details"

    Competitors must obey the height limits for their category: upper limits of 1000 m (Unlimited), 1100 m (Advanced) and 1200 m (Intermediate), and lower limits of 100 m (Unlimited) and 200 m (Advanced and Intermediate). Each figure flown completely below the lower limit costs 250 penalty points (Unlimited) or 200 (Advanced and Intermediate), and flying below the disqualification height (50 m for Unlimited, 100 m for Advanced and Intermediate) disqualifies the competitor from the programme. The floor depends on the category flown.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is below the floor of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch below is charged in proportion to how far below it is and for how much of the figure's duration, on a steeper scale than the other box limits. The rules apply fixed contest penalties rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

    The deduction does not reduce this figure's score. FCScore adds up the box deductions of all the figures of the sequence into one sequence-level Positioning mark, from 10 down to 0, and weights it with the schedule's Positioning K factor, as the judges' mark is weighted. The mark is continuous: FCScore does not round it to the steps the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, keeps the deduction on the figure instead.

> 4.3.5.1 Unlimited: b) In Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4, 250 penalty points will be given for each figure flown completely below the lower height limit. … 4.3.5.2 Advanced and Intermediate: b) 200 penalty points will be given for each figure flown completely below the lower height limit. … A competitor flying lower than the disqualification height (see 3.8.1.1) will be disqualified (from the current programme) for causing a dangerous situation.
>
> [4.3.5.1 b, 4.3.5.2 b](#rb-box.floor)

> The following height limitations have been determined for all contest flights: Category Upper Lower Disqualification; Unlimited 1000 m 100 m 50 m; Advanced 1100 m 200 m 100 m; Intermediate 1200 m 200 m 100 m
>
> [3.8.1.1](#rb-box.heights)

## Inter-element downgrades

### Loop Radius Matching {#inter.loop_radius}

`inter.loop_radius`

Checks that the looping lines in a figure that must have matching radii do match. Each radius is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Only certain figures require matching radii: all part-loops drawn as round elements in a figure share a radius (except the second loop of a Family 8.8 figure), and part-loops drawn as corners need not match except in Family 3 and Family 7.4 figures, where all part-loops must. CIVA-P gives no standardized downgrade for a mismatch.

    FCScore takes the radius of each looping line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, rather than with the first, charging in proportion to how many times larger one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the size. Whether each loop is round is judged by Loop Roundness.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> For any one figure having several internal part-loops depicted as round elements, all such part-loops shall have the same radius – with exception for all of Family 8.8 figures (double humpty bumps) for which the radius of the second part loop is not required to match the radius of the first one.
>
> [B.8.2.1 c](#rb-loops.matching_radii)

> The radius of any part-loop depicted as a corner angle is not required to match the radius of any other part-loop in the same figure – with exception for all of Family 3 (combinations of lines) and Family 7.4 (whole loops) figures, which must keep a regular geometrical shape and therefore require all part-loops to have the same radius.
>
> [B.8.2.1 d](#rb-loops.corner_radii)

### Line Length Matching {#inter.line_length}

`inter.line_length`

Checks that lines that must be of equal length in a figure are. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Interior lines do not have to be equal unless the figure says so, as in Family 3 and the square and octagon loops. Where equal lengths are required, the first line flown is the basis: a visible variation costs one point, a variation of 1:2 two points, and so on up to three points.

    FCScore takes the length of each line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length. FCScore's scale is smooth rather than in the rulebook's steps: it charges about one point for each whole multiple by which one line exceeds the other (one point at 2:1, two at 3:1, three at 4:1), which is close to the CIVA-P steps.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> An observed variation is penalised by reducing the mark in the following manner: a) a visible variation – one (1) point deduction; b) if the lengths vary by 1:2 – two (2) points deduction; c) and so forth up to a three (3) points deduction; d) No line before OR after roll – four (4) points deduction; e) No line before AND after roll – two (2) points deduction only
>
> [B.8.1.5](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, the basis for judging line length is the first line flown.
>
> [B.8.1.5](#rb-lines.length_basis)

### Roll Rate Matching {#inter.roll_rate}

`inter.roll_rate`

Checks that the rolls within one roll combination are flown at the same roll rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a hesitation roll the rate of roll, when not in pause, must be constant throughout. CIVA-P gives no numerical deduction for rates that differ, and does not require the rotation rates of unlinked rolls to match each other, so this is the rule it follows most closely for hesitation rolls.

    FCScore takes the roll rate of each roll within a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate. FCScore groups rolls by the figure definition rather than by the rule, so check the rulebook for your figure. Whether the rate is steady within one roll is judged by Roll Rate Consistency.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The rate of the roll, when not in pause, must be constant throughout with the aircraft projecting the pre-stated plane and direction of flight.
>
> [B.9.26.2](#rb-rolls.hesitation_rate)

### Pause Duration Matching {#inter.point_duration}

`inter.point_duration`

Checks that the pauses between the rolls or points of a roll combination last the same time. Each duration is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a hesitation roll the pauses must be of identical duration, and a pause that is not recognizable to the judge makes the figure a hard zero. CIVA-P gives no numerical deduction for pauses of different lengths. Unlinked rolls must also show a brief but perceptible pause between them.

    FCScore takes the duration of each pause in a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the duration.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The pauses will be of identical duration. … If a pause is not recognizable to a judge, the figure is marked a Hard Zero (HZ).
>
> [B.9.26.3](#rb-rolls.hesitation_pause)

> With unlinked rolls, no line links the symbols, though their tips are drawn pointing in the same direction (i.e., on the same side of the line). They must have a brief but perceptible pause between them and they are to be flown in the same direction of rotation.
>
> [B.9.24.4 c](#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause)

### Roll Position On Line {#inter.pad_length}

`inter.pad_length`

Checks that a roll is centred on its line, with equal lengths of line before and after it. The two lengths are compared and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    If any kind of roll is placed on an interior line (except when a roll follows a spin), the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal, with the same penalties as other equal-length lines.

    FCScore compares the length of line before the roll with the length after, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A roll that is perfectly centred scores zero, whatever the length of the line.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> Whenever any kind of roll is placed on an interior line (except when any type of roll follows a spin), the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal.
>
> [B.8.1.4](#rb-lines.length_equal)

> An observed variation is penalised by reducing the mark in the following manner: a) a visible variation – one (1) point deduction; b) if the lengths vary by 1:2 – two (2) points deduction; c) and so forth up to a three (3) points deduction; d) No line before OR after roll – four (4) points deduction; e) No line before AND after roll – two (2) points deduction only
>
> [B.8.1.5](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

## Sequence-level score

### Positioning {#presentation}

`presentation`

The sequence positioning mark for placing the figures optimally for the judges. FCScore estimates it from the box deductions of all the figures, added up and taken off 10.

??? note "Details"

    In CIVA-P each judge marks the figures that are not optimally placed (somewhat or considerably non-optimal) and combines the annotations into one sequence positioning mark: half a mark off for each 'somewhat' and a full mark for each 'considerably', and the judge may revise the result by up to one point. The mark has its own K factor, 40K for Unlimited and 30K for Advanced and Intermediate in Programmes 1 to 4.

    FCScore does not mark non-optimal figures. It adds up the box deductions of every figure (how far each figure strays outside the box boundaries, measured as the box downgrades describe) and takes the total off 10, so a figure that is flown outside the zone, or close to its edge, lowers the mark. The balance of the sequence about the secondary axis and the judge's revision are not modelled.

    The score is 10 minus the total of the figures' box deductions, with a lowest score of 0, and it is weighted by the schedule's Positioning K factor like an extra figure. A missing or failed figure adds nothing, because it already scores 0. The score is continuous, not rounded to the half points the judges use. A schedule with no Positioning K factor, such as a Freestyle programme, has no Positioning score and its figures keep their own box deductions.

> Positioning refers to the 3D placement of each figure relative to the performance zone and to the judges. A position mark will be given by each Judge.
>
> [4.1.5.1](#rb-positioning.marking)

> The position of a figure is somewhat or considerably “non-optimal” when it adversely affects the judge’s ability to assess it, is poorly positioned when considered within the design of the sequence, or its position dictates that subsequent figures will not be flown at optimal positions and may therefore be difficult to assess. Otherwise, the position shall be considered satisfactory, and no position downgrade is required.
>
> [4.1.5.4](#rb-positioning.non_optimal)

> At the end of the sequence the annotations in the “Pos” column shall be used by each judge to determine a sequence positioning downgrade based primarily on these recorded observations. Each single letter is taken as equivalent to a half mark and each double letter equivalent to a full mark downgrade. The Judge is entitled to revise his final positioning mark up or down by a maximum of one (1) point if he considers there were other relevant factors which should be taken into account to reduce or increase the downgrade.
>
> [4.1.5.7](#rb-positioning.downgrade)

> The K factor for positioning marks in Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4 will be as follows: a) Unlimited: 40K b) Advanced & Intermediate: 30K
>
> [4.1.5.8](#rb-positioning.k_factor)

> Consideration of all the parameters in the few short paragraphs of this section will enable a judge to make a clear decision about any figure that is clearly flown in other than its optimum position. Judging of the particular figure will be difficult, and such bad presentation should be reflected in the positioning mark for the sequence. It would be appropriate to deduct between half (0.5) and one (1) point for any such misplaced figure, depending on the severity of the difficulty incurred.
>
> [B.10.1.5](#rb-positioning.optimal)

Otherwise, the position shall be considered satisfactory, and no position downgrade is required.

The Judge is entitled to revise his final positioning mark up or down by a maximum of one (1) point if he considers there were other relevant factors which should be taken into account to reduce or increase the downgrade.

`box.ceiling`

> 4.3.5.1 Unlimited: c) For every climb above the upper height limit (see 3.8.1.1) in Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4, 50 penalty points will be given. … 4.3.5.2 Advanced and Intermediate: c) For every climb above the upper height limit (see 3.8.1.1), 30 penalty points will be given.

### 4.3.6.2, 4.3.6.3 {#rb-box.boundary_penalty}

`box.boundary_penalty`

> For each infringement of the performance zone in Programmes 1, 2, 3 and 4 by more than 50 metres in the direction of the main axis and/or the secondary axis a pilot will be given penalty points in accordance with the table below. Zone Infringement: Unlimited 30, Advanced or Intermediate 20 (Penalty point tariff). … Thereafter, for every figure started beyond 50 metres outside the performance zone, further penalty points will be given, in accordance with the same table.

### 4.4.1.2 {#rb-general.figure_start}

`general.figure_start`

> At the initiation or completion of every figure and at comparable moments within the figure, each deviation from a wings level, horizontal flight path with the aircraft longitudinal axis parallel to the relevant box axis, in accordance with paragraph B.6.1.1, will attract a reduction of half (0.5) point per 2.5 degrees of deviation, one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.

### 4.4.1.4 {#rb-general.angle_rule}

`general.angle_rule`

> All deviations from the correct geometry (plane of flight, direction of flight, angle of bank), and for deviations from the proper flight path or the proper attitude (as appropriate), the mark will be reduced by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation.

### 4.4.1.5 {#rb-general.corrections}

`general.corrections`

> Over-rotating a roll and rolling the wings back again must be penalised by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of over-rotation, even if the correct geometry is resumed afterwards, and no matter how quickly the correction is made.

### B.10.1.5 {#rb-positioning.optimal}

`positioning.optimal`

> Consideration of all the parameters in the few short paragraphs of this section will enable a judge to make a clear decision about any figure that is clearly flown in other than its optimum position. Judging of the particular figure will be difficult, and such bad presentation should be reflected in the positioning mark for the sequence. It would be appropriate to deduct between half (0.5) and one (1) point for any such misplaced figure, depending on the severity of the difficulty incurred.

### B.3.1.1 {#rb-general.flight_path}

`general.flight_path`

> Judging the flight path or the track over the ground consists of comparing the observed path with fixed references such as the horizon or the main and secondary axes of the Aerobatic Box.

### B.3.2.1 {#rb-lines.vertical}

`lines.vertical`

> Judging vertical lines is based on the attitude of the aircraft and not its flight path. … The aircraft's attitude while in this condition (zero lift) defines the proper judging criterion for vertical attitude. This is called the zero-lift axis.

### B.3.3.1 {#rb-lines.diagonal}

`lines.diagonal`

> This is the vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees. … The prescribed deduction is one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation from the correct geometry (0.5 points per 2.5 degrees).

### B.4.1.2 {#rb-general.grading}

`general.grading`

> It should be assumed that a competitor is going to fly a perfect figure, so a Judge starts with a mark of ten (10).

### B.4.1.3 {#rb-box.scorability}

`box.scorability`

> Should a competitor fly a figure at a location, inside or outside the performance zone, such that the accuracy of the flight path or attitude cannot reasonably be determined, a downgrade of two (2) points should be applied for each element of the figure that cannot be properly assessed.

### B.7.1.5 {#rb-general.wind_correction}

`general.wind_correction`

> A common flight mode is to crab into the wind as is done in navigational flight. … The downside to this approach is that if the aircraft longitudinal axis is detected by the Judge to be at an angle to the competition axis (main or secondary), a deduction of one (1) point per five (5) degrees will be given.

### B.8.1.1 {#rb-lines.heading}

`lines.heading`

> While maintaining a horizontal flight path, the aircraft's longitudinal axis must remain parallel to the main or secondary axis.

### B.8.1.1 {#rb-lines.horizontal}

`lines.horizontal`

> Horizontal lines in the vertical plane are judged on flight path, not attitude. … The deduction for deviation in either axis is one (1) point per five (5) degrees from the correct geometry.

### B.8.1.2 {#rb-general.no_line_between}

`general.no_line_between`

> All figures begin and end on definite horizontal lines, and both must be present in order to earn a good mark. A competitor who rushes from one figure to another without showing this horizontal and well-recognizable line will be downgraded by one (1) point for each missing line in each figure affected.

### B.8.1.4 {#rb-lines.length_equal}

`lines.length_equal`

> Whenever any kind of roll is placed on an interior line (except when any type of roll follows a spin), the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal.

### B.8.1.5 {#rb-lines.length_basis}

`lines.length_basis`

> If within a figure two or more lines must be of the same length, the basis for judging line length is the first line flown.

### B.8.1.5 {#rb-lines.length_penalty}

`lines.length_penalty`

> An observed variation is penalised by reducing the mark in the following manner: a) a visible variation – one (1) point deduction; b) if the lengths vary by 1:2 – two (2) points deduction; c) and so forth up to a three (3) points deduction; d) No line before OR after roll – four (4) points deduction; e) No line before AND after roll – two (2) points deduction only

### B.8.2.1 a {#rb-loops.radius}

`loops.radius`

> A loop must have, by definition, a constant radius.

### B.8.2.1 c {#rb-loops.matching_radii}

`loops.matching_radii`

> For any one figure having several internal part-loops depicted as round elements, all such part-loops shall have the same radius – with exception for all of Family 8.8 figures (double humpty bumps) for which the radius of the second part loop is not required to match the radius of the first one.

### B.8.2.1 d {#rb-loops.corner_radii}

`loops.corner_radii`

> The radius of any part-loop depicted as a corner angle is not required to match the radius of any other part-loop in the same figure – with exception for all of Family 3 (combinations of lines) and Family 7.4 (whole loops) figures, which must keep a regular geometrical shape and therefore require all part-loops to have the same radius.

### B.9.10.1 {#rb-loops.crosswind}

`loops.crosswind`

> This wind correction is only with regards to the roundness of the loop and not for the effect of any crosswind on the figure. Therefore, no deduction is given if the finish point is displaced relative to the start point in a direction perpendicular to the plane of the loop.

### B.9.10.2 {#rb-loops.crab_wings}

`loops.crab_wings`

> Loops must be flown with no visible crabbing and wings must be level at all times. The one (1) point for every five (5) degrees rule holds for both these cases.

### B.9.10.3 {#rb-loops.integrated_rolls}

`loops.integrated_rolls`

> If there is a roll or rolls at the apex of the loop, it must be centred in the loop and flown on the arc of the loop itself. Flying the roll on a line at the apex of the loop is at least a two (2) point downgrade. If the roll is not centred, it must be downgraded one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of the arc that it is off centred.

### B.9.10.4 {#rb-loops.radius_deductions}

`loops.radius_deductions`

> To better quantify deductions for irregularity of the radius of looping figures, the Judge divides the loop into quadrants. Any recognizable variation in the radius must be downgraded by a maximum of two (2) points per quadrant depending on the magnitude of the variation.

### B.9.2.2, B.9.2.5 a {#rb-turns.entry_bank}

`turns.entry_bank`

> This must be a roll of between 60 and 90 degrees, it must be performed on the entry heading, and the aircraft must maintain a constant horizontal line. … The angle of bank established by the initial rolling manoeuvre must be at least 60 degrees. Anything less is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees.

### B.9.2.5 b {#rb-turns.bank}

`turns.bank`

> The angle of bank, once established, must remain constant. Any deviation is a one (1) point deduction for every five (5) degrees of deviation.

### B.9.2.5 d {#rb-turns.altitude}

`turns.altitude`

> The aircraft must maintain a constant altitude throughout the figure. Any variation would be either one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of change or one (1) point for every 100 feet.

### B.9.2.5 e {#rb-turns.rate}

`turns.rate`

> The rate of turn must remain constant. Any change would be no more than a one (1) point deduction for each change.

### B.9.24.4 c {#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause}

`rolls.unlinked_pause`

> With unlinked rolls, no line links the symbols, though their tips are drawn pointing in the same direction (i.e., on the same side of the line). They must have a brief but perceptible pause between them and they are to be flown in the same direction of rotation.

### B.9.25.1 {#rb-rolls.rate}

`rolls.rate`

> The penalty for varying the rate of roll is one (1) point per variation. Any stoppage in the slow roll that could result in its being considered a hesitation roll, would Hard Zero (HZ) the figure.

### B.9.25.3 {#rb-rolls.stop}

`rolls.stop`

> The wings must stop precisely after the desired degree of rotation and not go past the stop point and then return. This is referred to as "bumping the point". A deduction of half (0.5) point to one (1) point is given depending on the severity of the "bump".

### B.9.26.2 {#rb-rolls.hesitation_rate}

`rolls.hesitation_rate`

> The rate of the roll, when not in pause, must be constant throughout with the aircraft projecting the pre-stated plane and direction of flight.

### B.9.26.3 {#rb-rolls.hesitation_pause}

`rolls.hesitation_pause`

> The pauses will be of identical duration. … If a pause is not recognizable to a judge, the figure is marked a Hard Zero (HZ).

### B.9.27.2, B.9.27.3 {#rb-snap_rolls.break}

`snap_rolls.break`

> The judge must see two things to determine that a flick roll has been correctly initiated: a) the aircraft must display a rapid and clearly visible change of pitch attitude (Figure 48) to put the wing close to the stall, and b) autorotation must be initiated by use of the rudder. … However, if the required pitch change and/or actual autorotation are not clearly seen, the mark must be downgraded by four (4) points. … At the start of a positive flick roll, the aircraft must clearly and unambiguously pitch in the nose up / tail down sense, from the pilot’s perspective, to put the wings near the critical angle-of-attack (Figure 48). If the aircraft pitches in the wrong direction, a Hard Zero (HZ) is given.

### B.9.27.3 {#rb-snap_rolls.definition}

`snap_rolls.definition`

> Either shortly after or simultaneously with the pitch change the aircraft must yaw, initiating a stall of one wing and the rapid onset of autorotation.

### B.9.27.3 {#rb-snap_rolls.pre_roll}

`snap_rolls.pre_roll`

> Provided the flick initiation criteria are satisfied, any roll that is observed before the autorotation starts must be downgraded by one (1) point per five (5) degrees of roll.

### B.9.27.4 {#rb-general.autorotation}

`general.autorotation`

> Throughout the flick the roll must be driven primarily by the rudder, and autorotation must be seen to continue. This can best be confirmed by the observed conical motion of the fuselage longitudinal axis, the largest displacement being at the tail which is furthest from the C of G.

### B.9.27.4 {#rb-snap_rolls.exit}

`snap_rolls.exit`

> For all aircraft types, the criteria for stopping the flick roll are the same: autorotation must stop at the desired extent of roll, followed immediately by adoption of the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. … Downgrades for errors in the extent of rotation or the following flight path or attitude are penalised at the normal rate of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of error.

### B.9.27.5 {#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation}

`snap_rolls.autorotation`

> A common error is for the aircraft initially to autorotate but to not stay in autorotation until the end of the figure, the roll becoming driven substantially by application of aileron; in this case a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees of rotation remaining when the autorotation ceases must be made. If autorotation ends with more than 45 degrees of rotation remaining, even if the roll is completed with aileron, the flick roll is awarded a numerical zero (0.0).

### B.9.28.1 {#rb-snap_rolls.negative}

`snap_rolls.negative`

> For negative flick rolls, all criteria stated for positive flick rolls apply except that the aircraft is in a negative rather than positive angle-of-attack during autorotation. Therefore, in a negative flick roll the nose and tail of the aircraft must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense, from the pilot’s perspective, as the angle-of-attack is changed (Figure 49).

### B.9.29.3, B.9.29.6 {#rb-spins.entry}

`spins.entry`

> When the aircraft stalls, the nose will fall and at the same time the wing tip will drop in the direction of the spin. Failure to achieve this should be considered a "forced entry" and downgraded one (1) point per five (5) degrees of deviation. … If the aircraft never stalls, it is apparent that it cannot spin, and a downgrade of four (4) points must be given.

### B.9.29.4 {#rb-spins.continue}

`spins.continue`

> Be alert for early stopping of the stalled autorotation followed by "aileroning" to the pre-stated heading. In this case, a deduction of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of "aileroning" must be applied.

### B.9.29.4 {#rb-spins.stop}

`spins.stop`

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the pre-stated heading, then a 90 degree down, wings-level attitude must be seen.

### B.9.29.5 {#rb-spins.attitude}

`spins.attitude`

> No account is to be taken of the pitch attitude of the aircraft during autorotation, as some aircraft spin in a nearly vertical pitch attitude while others spin quite flat in conventional spins. Speed of rotation is also not a judging criterion.

### B.9.29.7 {#rb-spins.definition}

`spins.definition`

> In all spins the grading criteria are: a) A clean breaking stall in horizontal flight. b) Fully stalled autorotation. c) Stopping on pre-stated heading. d) Vertical down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading. e) A constant, reasonable quarter-loop radius back the horizontal flight.

### B.9.29.7 d {#rb-spins.downline}

`spins.downline`

> Vertical down, wings-level attitude after stopping on heading.

### B.9.3.1 {#rb-turns.rolling}

`turns.rolling`

> The term “evenly integrated” means that from start to finish the figure should display a constant rate of turn combined with a constant rate of roll.

### B.9.3.6 d {#rb-turns.rolling_rate}

`turns.rolling_rate`

> Each variation in the rate of roll is no more than a one (1) point deduction.

### B.9.3.6 d, B.9.3.6 e {#rb-turns.rolling_stop}

`turns.rolling_stop`

> Each stoppage of the rate of roll is a deduction of two (2) points. … At a roll direction reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level. A longer pause is no more than a one (1) point deduction.

### B.9.3.6 e {#rb-turns.rolling_reversal}

`turns.rolling_reversal`

> At a roll direction reversal there must be only a short pause, with the wings level. A longer pause is no more than a one (1) point deduction. Errors in the roll angle from wings level are deducted using one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### B.9.5.1 {#rb-stall_turns.definition}

`stall_turns.definition`

> At the top of the vertical line, the aircraft pivots and establishes a vertical descent, with the figure ending as the aircraft is returned to horizontal flight.

### B.9.5.2 d {#rb-lines.vertical_wings}

`lines.vertical_wings`

> During the vertical climb or vertical descent, the wings must remain parallel to the horizon. There will be a one (1) point deduction per five (5) degrees of deviation of the vertical (yaw) axis from horizontal.

### B.9.5.2 e {#rb-stall_turns.pivot}

`stall_turns.pivot`

> As the aircraft nears the point where it would stop climbing, it must pivot in a plane parallel to vertical. Ideally, the aircraft pivots around its centre of gravity. … The downgrade for this deviation (often referred to as "flying over the top") is one (1) point per half wingspan that the point of rotation exceeds the maximum allowed (Pivot Point B, Figure 21).

### B.9.5.2 g {#rb-stall_turns.pivot_motion}

`stall_turns.pivot_motion`

> The wings must remain in the vertical geometric plane throughout the turnaround, and the aircraft's attitude before and after the turnaround must be absolutely vertical, with no pitch or roll. If there is movement around the roll axis, often referred to as "torquing" (Figure 22), there is a deduction of one (1) point for each five (5) degrees off axis.

### B.9.6.1 {#rb-tailslides.lean}

`tailslides.lean`

> The aircraft must slide in the vertical plane and not with the nose inclined towards the horizon. A slide of this type must be downgraded by the formula of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of inclination.

### B.9.6.1, 4.4.1.7 {#rb-tailslides.slide}

`tailslides.slide`

> At the point when the aircraft stops, it must slide backwards by at least a half fuselage length. If there is no slide of at least this length, the mark is downgraded by four (4) points. … A tail slide that does not move backwards by the required amount must be penalized by four (4) points.

### B.9.6.2 {#rb-tailslides.recovery}

`tailslides.recovery`

> Following the slide backwards, the aircraft must then tip over and fall through to a diving position.

### B.9.6.6 {#rb-tailslides.definition}

`tailslides.definition`

> In summary, the aircraft should make a smooth and steady transition up to vertical flight, the wings should stay level in relation to the horizon, and the aircraft should come to a complete stop in this attitude.
